transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Thank you. Well, I... I wasn't really sure if I should even make this appointment, to be completely honest with you. I've been working as a veterinary technologist for a long time now, and I've always prided myself on being able to handle a lot of stress. You know, dealing with sick animals, panicked owners, all the constant chaos of the clinic. I have a graduate degree, I’m 52, I feel like I should have my life figured out by now, right? But lately, everything just feels so incredibly heavy, and I just can't seem to shake it. I try to push through it, I really do, but it’s like wading through wet cement all day long, just exhausting. 

But... well, what actually scared me enough to finally pick up the phone and come in today is... my thoughts have gotten really dark. I go to bed at night and I just keep thinking that it would be so much easier if I just didn’t wake up. Just peaceful, you know? No more alarms, no more forcing myself to function. And then... sometimes, when I’m driving home from the clinic—there’s this one winding road I take every evening—I actually catch myself staring straight ahead and wondering what would happen if I just didn’t turn the wheel. If I just let the car keep going straight off the road. It completely terrifies me when I snap out of it, because I've always been a safe driver, but the thought is just so loud, and it keeps happening, and I just... I didn't know who else to talk to about it.
How long have you been feeling this way, with everything feeling heavy and having these dark thoughts?

Well, if I really sit down and trace it back to when it got this bad... it’s been about a month. A solid month of just... this intense, exhausting crisis. 

You see, we recently had to take in a relative of ours. It wasn't exactly planned, it was one of those sudden family emergencies where you don't really have a choice, you know? You just have to step up and do the right thing, and I’ve always been the one in the family who steps up. But bringing them into our home... it just completely upended absolutely everything. Our daily routines, our physical space, my ability to just sit in silence and decompress after a twelve-hour shift at the clinic. 

It’s just been this constant, unpredictable up-and-down situation every single day since they arrived. We had to scramble to clear out the spare room, which I was using to store some of my old graduate school materials and paperwork, and then we had to figure out all the logistics of their daily needs and integrating them into our household schedule. It's like I'm managing a second clinic the second I walk through my front door. One minute things seem like they might be stabilizing, and the next it's just chaos again. 

So, yeah, this unbearable heaviness, and those terrifying thoughts on the drive home... it all really started settling in and getting this loud over the last four weeks or so. Ever since this whole situation with our relative began, it's just been a month of non-stop crisis, and I just haven't had a single second to catch my breath.
Have you noticed any changes in your interest in activities that you used to enjoy?

Oh, gosh... yes. Yes, absolutely, and that’s honestly one of the things that bothers me the most right now, because it just highlights how wrong everything is. 

I used to... well, I’ve always been an avid amateur photographer, especially nature photography. I have this really nice camera setup that I used to take everywhere with me, sometimes even on my lunch breaks at the clinic just to get away and look for interesting shots of the local wildlife or the trees. But I haven't even touched my camera in weeks. It's just sitting in its bag in the hallway closet gathering dust, and I can't even bring myself to unzip the case. 

And the bird feeders! I have these feeders out in the backyard, and I used to be so meticulous about keeping them full and watching the cardinals and the chickadees come in every morning while I had my coffee. It was my little ritual before the chaos of the day started. Now, I look out the kitchen window and I see they're empty, and I just... I feel absolutely nothing. I don't check them with any real interest at all. If the squirrels get to them, I don't even care. 

I don't even care what's coming up in the garden, either. Usually, I'm out there checking the soil, planning out where the new perennials are going to go, seeing what survived the winter... but the thought of going out there just feels completely empty to me now. It’s just dirt and weeds. 

It’s actually really frightening to me, to be completely honest with you. It terrifies me because doing those things... being out in the yard, taking photos, tending to the garden... those things used to be how I felt like myself. That was my identity outside of work and outside of being the family caretaker. And without that, without caring about any of it, I just don't even know who I am right now.
Have you been experiencing any physical symptoms like rapid heartbeat, sweating, or trembling, especially when you're not thinking about those dark thoughts?

No, no, I wouldn't say I've had anything like that. No rapid heartbeat or sweating, nothing physical like that. I mean, my heart pounds when I get startled, obviously, like if a dog suddenly barks right next to me at the clinic when I'm not expecting it, or if someone drops a metal tray in the treatment area—that sound is just so sharp, it goes right through you, you know? But that's just a normal reaction, I think. That's not what you're asking about. 

As for just sitting there and suddenly sweating or trembling out of nowhere... no. It's really more of a... a profound heaviness, like I was saying before. It's not a racing, panicked feeling. It's the exact opposite, actually. It's this deep, crushing slowness. Like my body is just made of lead. 

Even when I'm not having those dark thoughts about the car or just not waking up, I'm not anxious or jittery. I'm just... drained. Utterly drained. So no, no trembling or anything like that. Just this constant, exhausting weight that I drag around with me everywhere I go, whether I'm at the clinic trying to draw blood from a squirming cat or just sitting on my couch trying to find the energy to make dinner for everyone. It's just the heaviness.
Have you been having any trouble sleeping?

Sleep... oh, sleep has just become this absolute nightmare, honestly. It used to be the one thing I could count on, you know? I’d get home, have a cup of tea, and just pass out because I was physically tired from wrestling golden retrievers all day. But now? Now it's just this agonizing process. 

I'll get into bed, and my body will feel like it weighs a thousand pounds, like I was telling you, but my brain just... it just turns on. And it's not even productive thoughts. I just lie there in the dark, staring at the ceiling fan, and I start replaying absolutely every single mistake I've ever made. I'll think about a blood draw I missed on a tiny kitten three weeks ago, or something I said to my husband that sounded sharper than I meant it to, or how I'm failing this relative we took in because I resent them being there. It just loops and loops and loops, and I'll look at the clock and it's 1:00 AM, then 2:30 AM, then 4:00 AM. 

And then, if I do finally manage to drift off out of pure exhaustion, I wake up before dawn. Like, 4:30 or 5:00 in the morning, my eyes just snap open. And I'm so incredibly tired. My bones ache with how tired I am. But I can't go back to sleep. I just lie there as the sun comes up, feeling completely depleted before the day has even started. 

Sometimes on my days off, I'll try to just stay in bed longer, hoping maybe if I just keep my eyes closed and stay horizontal, my body will somehow absorb some rest. I used to be a runner, you know—I'd get up and do three miles before my shift. But now, even if I stay in bed until 9:00 AM, I get up and I feel like I haven't slept in a week. I can't run. I can barely function enough to make a pot of coffee. It's like the sleep I am getting is entirely useless. It doesn't restore anything. It just feels like I'm slowly running out of battery, day after day, and I don't know how much longer I can keep functioning on this little actual rest before I just completely collapse at the clinic.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite recently?

My appetite... well, it's just been completely all over the place, honestly. It's like my stomach doesn't even know what it wants anymore, or if it wants anything at all. 

You know, we have this little break room at the clinic, and usually, it's the hub of everything. People are always bringing in bagels, or someone orders a couple of pizzas because it's been a crazy day with walk-in emergencies, and I used to be right in there with them. I'd always pack these nice, balanced lunches for myself—salads with grilled chicken, or leftovers from a roast I made the night before. I used to actually enjoy cooking and making sure everyone was fed. But lately... I just can't even stomach the thought of a full meal. 

Most mornings, I’ll force myself to make a piece of toast, maybe just dry toast or with a tiny scrape of butter, and I'll pour a cup of coffee. And I just kind of pick at the edges of the toast while I'm staring out the window at those empty bird feeders I mentioned earlier. I don't even finish it half the time. And then I go into work, and it's just back-to-back appointments, you know, wrestling a terrified German Shepherd for an exam, or monitoring anesthesia for dental cleanings, and the whole day just blurs by in this heavy haze. 

And then suddenly it's 6:00 PM, my shift is finally over, I'm taking off my scrubs in the locker room, and it suddenly hits me that I haven't eaten a single thing since that half a piece of toast at 5:30 in the morning. I've literally barely eaten all day. I've just been running on that one cup of coffee and whatever fumes I have left. 

And the strange thing is, even then, when I realize I haven't eaten for twelve hours, I'm still not really hungry. My stomach might feel a little hollow, but the idea of actually chewing and swallowing food just seems so incredibly exhausting. My husband keeps asking what I want for dinner when I get home, trying to be helpful, and I just have to tell him I don't care, I'm not hungry, just make whatever for him and the relative we're taking care of. Food just feels like cardboard to me right now. It's just another chore I don't have the energy for.
Do you often feel guilty or blame yourself for things that have happened, including the situation with your relative?

Oh, the guilt... it's just constant. It's honestly like this suffocating blanket on top of the heaviness I already feel. You mentioned the situation with our relative, and... I mean, that's really the crux of it right now. We took them in because it was supposed to be the right thing to do, you know? Family helping family. And I agreed to it. I wanted to be that supportive person. But honestly? I just resent it so deeply. I resent the disruption to our home, to our quiet space, to the routine I desperately need just to keep my head above water. 

And then, the moment I feel that resentment, this massive wave of guilt just crashes over me, and I keep telling myself I am just a terrible, terrible person for feeling that way. I mean, who does that? Who resents someone in their own family who just needs a place to stay and some help? 

I'll be sitting there in the living room, and I can literally feel my face setting into this rigid, annoyed expression. And like I was saying about lying awake at night, I just replay those moments over and over in my head. Every single impatient look I give them, every time I let out a heavy sigh when they ask me a perfectly normal question, every sharp, biting comment I make to my husband when he's just trying to keep the peace and make dinner... I replay all of it. 

And it just serves as this undeniable proof to me. It's proof that I'm completely toxic to be around right now. I look at how much tension I'm causing in my own house, how cold and unfeeling I've become, and I just think... they would honestly be so much better off without me. They really would. My husband wouldn't have to walk on eggshells or deal with this miserable, drained version of his wife, and our relative wouldn't have to feel like an imposition, which I know they do because I can't even hide my frustration properly. I just feel like I'm failing them on every conceivable level, and I'm just dragging my whole family down with me. It's just... it's a horrible way to feel about yourself, but I can't stop seeing all the evidence that I'm just making their lives worse.
Have you thought about how you would carry out those thoughts of not waking up or driving off the road if you were to act on them?

Well... that's the thing. That's actually the exact reason I'm sitting here talking to you today. Because it’s moved past just feeling tired or guilty. 

Like I was telling you about how horrible my sleep is, and how I just lie there in the dark for hours? Lately, when I’m lying there staring at the ceiling, I just keep thinking... I keep thinking it would be so much easier if I just didn’t wake up. If the sun came up and I just stayed asleep permanently, so I didn't have to face the clinic, or the tension with my husband, or the resentment toward our relative. It just sounds so peaceful to just... not exist tomorrow. 

But the driving part... that's what really terrified me. That's what scared me enough to actually pick up the phone and come in to see you. We live about twenty minutes from the veterinary clinic, and there's this one stretch of road on my commute home. It's usually dark by the time I leave because we always have late emergencies or I'm staying behind to clean up the surgical suite, and I'll be driving, just gripping the steering wheel, completely hollowed out from the day. And lately, I catch myself... I literally catch myself staring at the tree line or the steep drop-off on the shoulder, and I start wondering what would happen if I just didn't turn the wheel. 

Like, the curve is coming up, and my brain just says, "What if you just keep your foot on the gas and let the car go straight?" I can picture it so clearly. I don't know if I have this grand, detailed plan where I've written out a note or anything like that, but the fact that the thought is just right there, sitting in the passenger seat with me while I'm driving... it just terrified me. I’ve never had thoughts that felt that heavy or that tempting before. It’s just this constant, whispering thought that if I just let go of the wheel, I wouldn't have to feel this exhausted anymore.
Have you been having trouble concentrating on your work at the clinic or on anything else that requires your attention?

Concentrating? You know, you would really think so, wouldn't you? With everything I just told you about not sleeping and barely eating and just feeling so completely hollowed out... but, honestly? No. Not really. It's actually the one thing that hasn't completely fallen apart on me. 

When I'm at the clinic, it's almost like... I don't know, like a switch flips, or maybe it's just pure muscle memory at this point after doing it for so many years. Like just yesterday, we had this incredibly complicated dental extraction on a senior cat, a little hyperthyroid kitty, and I had to monitor the anesthesia. And with those older cats, you have to be so incredibly precise. You're watching the drip rates, monitoring their vitals, looking for every little dip in their heart rate or oxygen levels, and I was just... I was completely locked in. I didn't miss a single beat. I was calculating the medication dosages in my head just as fast as I always do, double-checking the charts, making sure the vet had exactly the right instruments ready before she even asked for them. 

It's strange, isn't it? I mean, I can barely figure out what to say to my husband when I get home, and the thought of deciding what to make for dinner or even just eating a piece of toast feels like climbing a mountain, but put a syringe in my hand or ask me to run a full blood panel on the machines in the back, and I can focus perfectly fine. I guess work is just this highly structured environment where I don't have to think about myself, or the tension with our relative, or how miserable and guilty I feel. I just follow the protocols. The animals need me to be precise, so I am. 

So, no, my attention to detail is definitely still there. I'm not dropping the ball or making mistakes at work, even though I feel like I'm dragging a hundred-pound weight around with me while I'm doing it. I still read the labels, I still update the logs perfectly. It’s just... it's everything else outside of those specific, clinical tasks that feels completely impossible to focus on. But the actual work? No, my concentration there is completely fine.
Are you able to experience any pleasure or enjoyment from things that you normally find pleasurable?

Pleasure? Enjoyment? No. I mean, honestly, no. It's like that part of my brain just shut off completely, and they locked the door and threw away the key. 

Take my photography, for example. I have this really nice DSLR camera that my husband got me a few years ago. I used to take it everywhere, especially out into the yard on the weekends. I'd spend hours just waiting for the perfect lighting, adjusting the lenses, trying to get these really detailed macro shots of the flowers or the insects. But I haven't even touched my camera in... I don't even know how long. It's just sitting there in its case on the shelf in the living room, gathering dust. I look at it and I just feel absolutely nothing. No desire to pick it up, no spark, just... dead weight.

And the bird feeders... I used to be so meticulous about them. I have four different feeders set up in the backyard. Suet for the woodpeckers, thistle for the finches, black oil sunflower seeds for the cardinals, you know, the whole setup. I used to love sitting by the window with my coffee in the morning and just watching them. It brought me so much peace before heading into the chaos of the clinic. But now? I barely even check them. I think they've been empty for over a week, and the squirrels have probably ruined the baffles, but when I do look out the window, I just don't care. I don't look at them with any real interest at all. 

It's the exact same story with the garden. Spring is usually my favorite time because I get to plan out the beds and see what's coming up. I usually have all these heirloom tomatoes and zinnias planned out, and I'd be out there every evening pulling weeds and checking the soil. But right now... I just don't care what's coming up in the garden. The weeds are probably taking over the raised beds, the soil is probably dry, and I can't bring myself to even walk out the back door to look at it. 

And honestly, doctor, that's what is so incredibly frightening to me about all of this. Because those things—the photography, the birds, the gardening—those were my things. That used to be how I felt like myself, you know? It was how I decompressed and remembered who I was outside of being a vet tech or a wife or someone dealing with all this terrible tension in my house. And now it's all just gone. It's like the color has been completely drained out of my entire life. I keep waiting to wake up and feel that little pull to go outside and take a picture of a blue jay or check on the seedlings, but the pull just isn't there. It's just flat. Everything is just completely flat and gray, and it terrifies me because I just don't know who I am if I don't care about those things anymore. I just sit there and stare at the wall instead.
Do you feel like you have enough energy to perform your daily tasks?

Energy? Oh, doctor, no. Not at all. I mean, I honestly don't even remember what having energy actually feels like at this point. It's like my battery is permanently stuck at one percent, no matter what I do. 

Just to give you an idea of how bad it is... at the clinic, we have this setup where the main treatment area is right in the center of the building, and the lab benches where we run all the diagnostics are just down this short little hallway in the back. It's really not far at all, maybe twenty or thirty feet at the absolute most? I’ve walked back and forth down that hall a hundred times a day for years. But lately... lately, just the physical act of walking from the treatment area to the lab benches feels like I am literally dragging myself through waist-deep mud. I'll be holding something so light, you know, just a tiny little purple-top tube for a CBC, and my legs feel like they are made of solid lead. They feel like they weigh a thousand pounds each. I have to mentally coach myself just to lift my foot and take a step, and then another step, and I'm just praying none of the other techs stop me to ask a question because even just standing there holding myself upright to talk takes more physical stamina than I have in my entire body. 

And then, by the time I actually get through the shift and survive that awful drive home I was telling you about, I am just completely and utterly depleted. There is absolutely nothing left in the tank. When I walk through the front door, I can barely even manage to make dinner. And I'm not talking about cooking a huge meal from scratch, I mean even just standing at the microwave or putting a piece of bread in the toaster feels like this monumental, impossible task. 

And it makes everything at home so much harder, because I can barely help out with the evening care routine. You know, with the relative I mentioned earlier, the one causing all the tension? There's a whole routine in the evenings to get them settled, and my husband really needs my help with it, but I physically just... I can't. I just want to collapse onto the sofa in my scrubs and not move a single muscle until the next morning. I feel so incredibly guilty watching my husband do it all himself, knowing I should be up there helping him, but my body just refuses to go. It's like gravity is pulling me down into the floor and I just don't have the strength to fight it anymore.
Do you find yourself moving or reacting more slowly than you used to?

Moving slower? Reacting slowly? I mean, I know I just went on and on about feeling like my legs are made of lead and how exhausting it is just to walk down the hall, but... actually moving in slow motion? Or having delayed reactions? No, I really don't think so. I haven't noticed anything like that. 

If anything, when I actually have to move, I move just as fast as I always have. You really have to have lightning reflexes in veterinary medicine, you just do. Because if a frightened German Shepherd suddenly thrashes during a blood draw, or a feral cat tries to bolt off the exam table while you're trying to scruff it, you absolutely cannot be slow. If you're slow, you get bitten, or the animal gets hurt, or you lose a sterile field. Just the other day, Dr. Evans—she's our senior veterinarian at the practice—she accidentally bumped a mayo stand during a prep, and a whole tray of sterilized instruments started to slide off. I reached out and caught it before it even hit the floor. I didn't even have to think about it, my hand just shot out. So my reaction time is definitely still there. I haven't been bitten, I haven't dropped anything, and I'm not fumbling with the equipment. 

And it's the same at home, really. No one has told me I look like I'm moving sluggishly or talking slower. When my husband asks me a question about the house or about his relative, I answer him right away. I'm not sitting there staring blankly for five minutes trying to process what he just said before I speak. I hear him, I understand it immediately, and I respond at a totally normal speed, even if my response is just that I'm too tired to deal with it. 

So it’s not that my body or my brain are actually operating on a delay. It’s more like... the engine is running fine, the gears turn at the exact same speed they always have, there's just absolutely no gas in the tank to keep them going. Does that make sense? The physical heaviness is there, but the actual speed of my movements and my reflexes? No, those are perfectly fine. I haven't noticed any slow-down there at all.
Do you find yourself fidgeting or feeling restless when you're sitting still?

Fidgeting? Oh, no. No, definitely not. If anything, it's the exact opposite of that. When I finally sit down, I am completely, utterly still. Like, disturbingly still. 

You know how some people, when they're stressed or anxious, they bounce their leg or they pick at their cuticles or they pace around the room? We see it all the time at the clinic with the pet owners in the waiting room. They'll be waiting for bloodwork results on their golden retriever or their tabby cat, and they're just wearing a hole in the linoleum pacing back and forth, wringing their hands, constantly checking their phones, shifting in those hard plastic chairs we have out front. I see that nervous energy all day long. But me? No. I don't do any of that. 

When I get home and I finally sit down on that sofa in the living room—the brown one right across from the TV that we rarely even turn on anymore—I just sink into the cushions and I do not move a single muscle. I don't tap my fingers on the armrest, I don't bounce my knee, I don't even adjust my posture to get more comfortable. I just sit there. My husband will come downstairs after dealing with his relative's evening routine, and he'll walk into the living room and just look at me, and I know he's probably wondering if I'm even awake because I'm just staring straight ahead at the wall, completely motionless. 

It's like all the kinetic energy in my body has just totally evaporated. I don't have the urge to get up and pace, I don't feel jittery or restless in my skin. There's no nervous energy inside me at all, just this giant, heavy void. I honestly wish I had enough energy to fidget or feel restless, because at least that would mean there was some kind of spark or life left in there, you know? Like the engine was at least trying to turn over. But there isn't. I just sit there like a stone statue for hours, completely frozen in place, until I finally force myself to get up and go to bed. So, no, no fidgeting at all.
Have you ever thought of a specific plan for how you would end your life if you were to act on those thoughts of not waking up or driving off the road?

A specific plan... I mean, I haven't gone out and bought anything, or written out a note or set a date, if that's what you're asking. But... honestly, doctor, what actually scared me enough to finally pick up the phone and come in to see you today is how real those thoughts are becoming. 

I just keep thinking, over and over again, that it would be so much easier if I just didn’t wake up. When I finally drag myself into bed at night, after dealing with the clinic and the house and just the sheer weight of existing, I close my eyes and I just pray that I don't open them again. I think about how peaceful it would be to just slip away in my sleep and never have to face another morning, never have to force my legs out of bed, never have to deal with my husband's relative or another shift at the lab. 

But the part that really terrified me, the part that made me realize I couldn't just ignore this anymore... is the driving. I told you about that awful commute home from the clinic. Well, there's this one specific stretch on my route, right where the road curves sharply near the old highway overpass. I've driven it a thousand times. But lately, when I'm coming up on that bend, and I'm just so completely, utterly empty... I catch myself staring at the concrete barrier. And I actually catch myself wondering what would happen if I just didn't turn the wheel. 

It wouldn't even take any effort, you know? That's the scary part. It would actually take less effort than making the turn. I wouldn't have to do anything at all except just... relax my hands. Just let the car keep going straight. I sit there gripping the steering wheel, going sixty miles an hour, and my brain is just whispering, "Just let go. Just let it drift. It will all be over in a second." And the fact that I am sitting there, in my car, seriously contemplating just letting myself crash into a wall because I am too tired to turn the steering wheel... that scared me. It really scared me. Because it doesn't feel like just a passing thought anymore, it feels like a temptation. And I'm starting to not trust myself on that drive home.
Do you feel like you're moving slower than usual when you're doing everyday activities?

I know we touched on this just a little bit ago when you asked about my reflexes, but no, not for everyday things either. I really haven't noticed any actual slowing down of my movements, whether I'm at the clinic or just... just doing normal things around the house. 

I mean, take something as simple as making coffee in the morning. I don't stand there moving my arms in slow motion to scoop the coffee grounds into the filter. I scoop them just as fast as I did five or ten years ago. It's just that standing there in the kitchen feels like I'm wearing a lead suit. But the actual physical speed of my arm reaching into the canister? That's completely normal. 

It's the exact same thing with grocery shopping, or... or folding the laundry. When I finally get around to doing the laundry, I'm not moving like a turtle. I fold the towels and my husband's shirts at a perfectly normal, regular pace. I just... I might sit on the edge of the bed for an hour before I can convince myself to actually reach into the laundry basket to get started. The initiation part is what's broken. But once my hands are actually moving, they move right along just like they always have. I don't walk down the grocery aisles at half-speed, I don't brush my teeth in slow motion. I just want to get those things done and over with as fast as humanly possible so I can go sit back down. So, no, the actual physical speed of my movements during everyday activities hasn't slowed down at all. It's just the energy to start them that's missing.
Do you feel like your thoughts are moving slower than usual?

My thoughts? No, I wouldn't say they're moving slower. I mean, if anything, they're just... stuck. It's not that they're sluggish or taking a long time to process things. It's more like... like a record skipping on the same awful groove, over and over again. 

I'll be sitting there on that brown sofa I mentioned, the one across from the TV, and my brain isn't moving in slow motion. It's just entirely consumed by this heavy, dark loop. Like, I'll think about how exhausted I am, and then I'll think about having to get up for work the next day, and then I'll think about the commute and the concrete barrier, and then I'm right back to how exhausted I am. It just cycles through those same miserable thoughts at a perfectly normal speed, honestly. 

At the clinic, it's the same thing. When I'm running bloodwork or analyzing a sample under the microscope, my brain is processing the information just fine. I know exactly what I'm looking at, I know what the results mean, I know what to tell the vet. I'm not sitting there staring at a slide for five minutes trying to figure out what a white blood cell is. My cognitive function, or whatever you want to call it, is perfectly intact. It's just that underneath all of that, there's this constant, overwhelming soundtrack of just... emptiness. 

It's like my brain is a computer that's running perfectly fast, but it's only running one terrible program. I'm not struggling to find words or having trouble following a conversation. If my husband asks me what we should do about his relative's dinner, I don't have to sit there and slowly piece together a sentence. I just tell him I don't care, because I genuinely don't. The thought process itself is immediate. It's the content of the thoughts that's the problem, not the speed. I'm just so hyper-focused on how awful everything feels that there isn't room for anything else. So, no, they aren't moving slower. They're just trapped.
Are you able to enjoy or find pleasure in any activities or things that you normally would?

Enjoyment? No. Honestly, no, not at all. It's actually one of the things that bothers me the most, if I really think about it, because it just highlights how empty everything has become. 

I used to have hobbies, things that I genuinely loved doing when I wasn't at the clinic. I have this really nice camera, for instance. I used to love photography, just taking it out on the weekends and walking around, looking for the perfect lighting or an interesting angle on something completely ordinary. But now... I haven't even touched my camera in months. It's just sitting in its case on the shelf in the living room, gathering dust. I look at it and I just feel absolutely nothing. Not even a tiny spark of wanting to pick it up, let alone actually go outside and use it. 

And it's the exact same way with the birds. We have these big bird feeders out in the backyard, right outside the kitchen window. I used to be so meticulous about them, making sure they were filled with the right kind of seed—black oil sunflower seeds for the cardinals, suet for the woodpeckers. I used to stand at the window with my morning coffee just watching them, learning their patterns. But lately? I haven't checked the bird feeders with any real interest at all. My husband has been filling them because he knows I haven't been doing it, and I'll look out the window, but I'm just looking right past them. The birds are out there fluttering around, and I just don't care. It doesn't bring me that little moment of peace it used to. 

Even the yard work... usually, I'd be out there planning things out, but I haven't cared at all what’s coming up in the garden. Energy? Oh, doctor, no. Not at all. I mean, I honestly don't even remember what having energy actually feels like at this point. It's like my battery is permanently stuck at one percent, no matter what I do. 

Just to give you an idea of how bad it is... at the clinic, we have this setup where the main treatment area is right in the center of the building, and the lab benches where we run all the diagnostics are just down this short little hallway in the back. It's really not far at all, maybe twenty or thirty feet at the absolute most? I’ve walked back and forth down that hall a hundred times a day for years. But lately... lately, just the physical act of walking from the treatment area to the lab benches feels like I am literally dragging myself through waist-deep mud. I'll be holding something so light, you know, just a tiny little purple-top tube for a CBC, and my legs feel like they are made of solid lead. They feel like they weigh a thousand pounds each. I have to mentally coach myself just to lift my foot and take a step, and then another step, and I'm just praying none of the other techs stop me to ask a question because even just standing there holding myself upright to talk takes more physical stamina than I have in my entire body. 

And then, by the time I actually get through the shift and survive that awful drive home I was telling you about, I am just completely and utterly depleted. There is absolutely nothing left in the tank. When I walk through the front door, I can barely even manage to make dinner. And I'm not talking about cooking a huge meal from scratch, I mean even just standing at the microwave or putting a piece of bread in the toaster feels like this monumental, impossible task. 

And it makes everything at home so much harder, because I can barely help out with the evening care routine. You know, with the relative I mentioned earlier, the one causing all the tension? There's a whole routine in the evenings to get them settled, and my husband really needs my help with it, but I physically just... I can't. I just want to collapse onto the sofa in my scrubs and not move a single muscle until the next morning. I feel so incredibly guilty watching my husband do it all himself, knowing I should be up there helping him, but my body just refuses to go. It's like gravity is pulling me down into the floor and I just don't have the strength to fight it anymore.

Or having delayed reactions? No, I really don't think so. I haven't noticed anything like that. 

If anything, when I actually have to move, I move just as fast as I always have. You really have to have lightning reflexes in veterinary medicine, you just do. Because if a frightened German Shepherd suddenly thrashes during a blood draw, or a feral cat tries to bolt off the exam table while you're trying to scruff it, you absolutely cannot be slow. If you're slow, you get bitten, or the animal gets hurt, or you lose a sterile field. Just the other day, Dr. Evans—she's our senior veterinarian at the practice—she accidentally bumped a mayo stand during a prep, and a whole tray of sterilized instruments started to slide off. I reached out and caught it before it even hit the floor. I didn't even have to think about it, my hand just shot out. So my reaction time is definitely still there. I haven't been bitten, I haven't dropped anything, and I'm not fumbling with the equipment. 

And it's the same at home, really. No one has told me I look like I'm moving sluggishly or talking slower. When my husband asks me a question about the house or about his relative, I answer him right away. I'm not sitting there staring blankly for five minutes trying to process what he just said before I speak. I hear him, I understand it immediately, and I respond at a totally normal speed, even if my response is just that I'm too tired to deal with it. 

So it’s not that my body or my brain are actually operating on a delay. It’s more like... the engine is running fine, the gears turn at the exact same speed they always have, there's just absolutely no gas in the tank to keep them going. Does that make sense? The physical heaviness is there, but the actual speed of my movements and my reflexes? No, those are perfectly fine. I haven't noticed any slow-down there at all.

It's like all the kinetic energy in my body has just totally evaporated. I don't have the urge to get up and pace, I don't feel jittery or restless in my skin. There's no nervous energy inside me at all, just this giant, heavy void. I honestly wish I had enough energy to fidget or feel restless, because at least that would mean there was some kind of spark or life left in there, you know? Like the engine was at least trying to turn over. But there isn't. I just sit there like a stone statue for hours, completely frozen in place, until I finally force myself to get up and go to bed. A specific plan... I mean, I haven't gone out and bought anything, or written out a note or set a date, if that's what you're asking. But... honestly, doctor, what actually scared me enough to finally pick up the phone and come in to see you today is how real those thoughts are becoming. 

I just keep thinking, over and over again, that it would be so much easier if I just didn’t wake up. When I finally drag myself into bed at night, after dealing with the clinic and the house and just the sheer weight of existing, I close my eyes and I just pray that I don't open them again. But lately, when I'm coming up on that bend, and I'm just so completely, utterly empty... I catch myself staring at the concrete barrier. Just let the car keep going straight. I sit there gripping the steering wheel, going sixty miles an hour, and my brain is just whispering, "Just let go. Just let it drift. And the fact that I am sitting there, in my car, seriously contemplating just letting myself crash into a wall because I am too tired to turn the steering wheel... that scared me. Not even a tiny spark of wanting to pick it up, let alone actually go outside and use it. 

And it's the exact same way with the birds. We have these big bird feeders out in the backyard, right outside the kitchen window. I used to be so meticulous about them, making sure they were filled with the right kind of seed—black oil sunflower seeds for the cardinals, suet for the woodpeckers. I used to stand at the window with my morning coffee just watching them, learning their patterns. But lately? I haven't checked the bird feeders with any real interest at all. My husband has been filling them because he knows I haven't been doing it, and I'll look out the window, but I'm just looking right past them. The birds are out there fluttering around, and I just don't care. It doesn't bring me that little moment of peace it used to. 

Even the yard work... usually, I'd be out there planning things out, but I haven't cared at all what’s coming up in the garden. I used to spend hours with my hands in the dirt, figuring out where the perennials needed to be divided or what to plant in the front beds. And that... doctor, that is really, truly frightening to me. Because those things—the photography, the birds, the gardening—those things used to be how I felt like myself. They were my identity outside of being a technician or a wife. And now that I don't care about them anymore, it's like I don't even know who I am. I'm just this tired, empty person going through the motions, and all the things that used to bring color into my life are just completely gray. I just don't understand where all that joy went, you know? It's like it just evaporated into thin air, and I don't know how to get it back.
